title: Physical Neural Networks Need Nonlinearity, Amplification, and Suppression for Learning
summary: The exponential growth in energy consumption of artificial intelligence systems has spurred interest in physical computing paradigms that exploit the relaxation of physical systems toward steady states. However, many existing physical networks are fundamentally linear and incapable of performing nonlinear operations crucial for meaningful machine learning tasks. Here we use simulations to show that nonlinearity alone is insufficient; physical learning systems must also support signal amplification and suppression to perform nontrivial computations. We present physically plausible circuit designs that incorporate these essential features, enabling effective nonlinear information processing. Our findings clarify the limitations of linear physical networks and provide guidance for developing energy-efficient physical learning architectures capable of general machine learning tasks.

AI.tldr: Physical learning systems require not just nonlinearity but also signal amplification and suppression to perform meaningful computations, as demonstrated through simulations of novel circuit designs.
AI.motivation: The exponential growth in energy consumption of AI systems motivates the exploration of energy-efficient physical computing paradigms that exploit relaxation toward steady states, but existing physical networks are often linear and cannot perform nonlinear operations essential for machine learning.
AI.method: Simulations were used to demonstrate that nonlinearity alone is insufficient, and physically plausible circuit designs incorporating signal amplification and suppression were presented.
AI.result: Nonlinearity alone is insufficient for nontrivial computations; physical learning systems must also support signal amplification and suppression.
AI.conclusion: Linear physical networks have fundamental limitations, and incorporating amplification/suppression into physical learning architectures can enable energy-efficient general machine learning tasks.

title: Dissipative Quantum Multiplicative Weights with Sampling Feedback: A Classically Hard Primitive Realized via Engineered Open-System Dynamics
comment: main manuscript 10 pages, 9 figrues, appendixes 19 pages
summary: We introduce \emph{Dissipative Quantum Multiplicative Weights with Sampling Feedback} (DQMW-Sample), an online-learning primitive in which engineered open quantum-system dynamics prepare a Gibbs state whose computational-basis measurement supplies the loss feedback. The central conceptual contribution is to lift the computational hardness of constant-temperature Gibbs sampling into a physically realizable online-learning primitive. By engineering a Davies-type dissipator whose per-round feedback cannot be efficiently simulated classically, we obtain a learning-theoretic separation in which DQMW-Sample achieves asymptotically sublinear regret while every efficient classical learner suffers constant average regret on a suitably constructed instance. We further prove that the spectral gap of the engineered dissipator contracts hardware noise, yielding sublinear noise-induced regret under a balanced dissipation schedule, and we strengthen the single-round hardness to the full adaptive interaction: an efficient classical simulator of the entire $T$-round feedback process would collapse the polynomial hierarchy. We state the required realizability assumption in explicit form and report an initial hardware characterization on the IBM Heron~r2 processor. These results position DQMW-Sample as a concrete route toward computational advantage in online learning that is grounded in complexity theory and compatible with near-term superconducting hardware.

AI.tldr: DQMW-Sample is a quantum online-learning primitive that uses engineered open-system dynamics to prepare Gibbs states, achieving asymptotically sublinear regret while efficient classical learners suffer constant regret, with hardware demonstration on IBM Heron r2.
AI.motivation: To lift the computational hardness of constant-temperature Gibbs sampling into a physically realizable online-learning primitive, establishing a learning-theoretic separation between quantum and classical learners.
AI.method: Engineers a Davies-type dissipator whose per-round feedback cannot be efficiently simulated classically; uses dissipative quantum multiplicative weights with sampling feedback; employs a balanced dissipation schedule for noise-induced regret control.
AI.result: DQMW-Sample achieves asymptotically sublinear regret while every efficient classical learner suffers constant average regret on a constructed instance. The spectral gap contracts hardware noise, yielding sublinear noise-induced regret. An efficient classical simulator of the full T-round feedback process would collapse the polynomial hierarchy.
AI.conclusion: DQMW-Sample offers a concrete, complexity-theoretically grounded route toward computational advantage in online learning compatible with near-term superconducting hardware.

title: Criterion for qubit-assisted quantum metrology approaching Heisenberg scaling
summary: We study in this work the metrology precision of a probe system coupled to an ancillary qubit. Restricting the probe-qubit coupling along only one or two directions is found to be a sufficient criterion for the effective dynamical generator to achieve the Heisenberg limit in precision. Under the criterion, the quantum Fisher information (QFI) about the to-be-estimated parameter becomes the expectation value of mean square of the effective generator with respect to the initial state of the composite system. Our criterion is justified in two distinct systems. For a bosonic probe, QFI about the displacement estimation is found to be proportional to the mean excitation number of probe. It renders a counterintuitive result that quantum metrology sensitivity can be enhanced by increasing the temperature of the probe system. For a spin-ensemble probe, QFI about both rotation-phase and magnetic-field estimation exhibit a quadratic dependence on the probe-spin number. It is found that even when the spin-ensemble is prepared as a finite-temperature state, faraway from the so-called resource states, e.g., the squeezed state or the Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger state, QFI can still manifest a Heisenberg scaling behavior.

AI.tldr: The paper establishes a criterion for achieving Heisenberg-limited metrology precision in a probe system coupled to an ancillary qubit, showing that coupling along only one or two directions suffices. It demonstrates counterintuitive results: for bosonic probes, sensitivity increases with temperature; for spin-ensemble probes, Heisenberg scaling emerges even in finite-temperature states far from conventional resource states.
AI.motivation: To explore metrology precision limits of a probe system coupled to an ancillary qubit and identify sufficient conditions for achieving Heisenberg scaling beyond traditional resource states.
AI.method: Restricting probe-qubit coupling to one or two directions as a criterion for the effective dynamical generator to reach the Heisenberg limit; analyzed via quantum Fisher information (QFI) in two distinct systems: a bosonic probe (displacement estimation) and a spin-ensemble probe (rotation-phase and magnetic-field estimation).
AI.result: For bosonic probes, QFI for displacement estimation is proportional to the mean excitation number, implying sensitivity can be enhanced by increasing temperature. For spin-ensemble probes, QFI shows quadratic dependence on probe-spin number for both rotation-phase and magnetic-field estimation, with Heisenberg scaling behavior persisting even in finite-temperature states far from squeezed or GHZ states.
AI.conclusion: The criterion of restricted probe-qubit coupling (one or two directions) is sufficient for Heisenberg-limited precision, and counterintuitively, thermal noise can enhance sensitivity in bosonic probes while Heisenberg scaling survives in finite-temperature spin ensembles without requiring traditional resource states.

title: Interpretable rule-based learning in an autonomous thermodynamic network
comment: 12 pages + 3 pages of Appendices + 3 pages of Suppl. Materials; 5 figures + 2 in the Suppl. Materials
summary: Machine learning is typically described in terms of deterministic logical operations, whereas physical systems generally operate in the presence of noise, dissipation and irreversibility. Here, we turn these physical effects into computational resources for an autonomous, interpretable learning architecture. We develop a classifier based on thermodynamic neurons, which are autonomous quantum thermal machines that implement logical operations through heat flow, and use these to construct a stochastic version of the Tsetlin machine, an interpretable rule-based learning architecture. By combining thermodynamic AND, NOT and OR gates with an autonomous coupling mechanism, we realise a learning system whose computation unfolds without the need for external time-dependent control. Despite its noisy components, the resulting classifier achieves classification accuracy that is statistically comparable to that of the standard Tsetlin machine. Reliability arises from architectural mechanisms such as thresholding and redundancy, rather than exact logical operations. Our results highlight that accurate and interpretable learning can emerge from autonomous stochastic dynamics, and establish thermodynamic computation as a viable framework for physical machine learning.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a thermodynamic neuron-based classifier that uses noisy, dissipative physical processes (quantum thermal machines) to implement a stochastic Tsetlin machine, achieving classification accuracy comparable to its deterministic counterpart without external control.
AI.motivation: To turn noise, dissipation, and irreversibility—typically considered detrimental in physical systems—into computational resources for autonomous, interpretable machine learning.
AI.method: The authors construct thermodynamic neurons (autonomous quantum thermal machines) that implement AND, NOT, and OR gates via heat flow, combine them with an autonomous coupling mechanism, and build a stochastic version of the Tsetlin machine—a rule-based, interpretable learning architecture.
AI.result: The classifier achieves classification accuracy statistically comparable to the standard Tsetlin machine, despite operating with noisy components. Reliability comes from architectural mechanisms like thresholding and redundancy rather than exact logic.
AI.conclusion: Accurate and interpretable learning can emerge from autonomous stochastic dynamics, and thermodynamic computation offers a viable framework for physical machine learning.

title: A fidelity metric for quantum annealing benchmarked by extreme scaling quantum Monte-Carlo simulations
summary: Quantum annealers are supposed to follow adiabatically the ground state of a system as its Hamiltonian slowly interpolates between a trivial phase and a non-trivial one; the non-trivial ground state being the solution to an optimization problem. Overwhelmingly, their performances are measured in terms of how well or fast the optimization problem is solved. While pragmatic, this approach is inherently brittle as it strongly depends on the problem considered and the classical algorithm used as the reference benchmark. Here, we propose a quantity that not only measures the end result but also the quality of the actual quantum annealing process itself. Our metric is the quantum annealing counterpart of the fidelity-per gate of gate-based quantum computers. It takes the form of an accuracy $ε$ for the equation of state of the annealer. We calculate benchmark values of $ε$ using two variants of the simulated quantum annealing technique for Rydberg atoms systems. Our first approach uses variational quantum Monte-Carlo with an ansatz inspired by thermal annealing. It suggests that within $ε\sim 10^{-2}-10^{-3}$, a quantum annealer is indistinguishable from its thermal classical counterpart. Critically, we could reach this precision up to $100,000,000$ atoms on a single CPU. Our second approach (based on Green function quantum Monte-Carlo) reaches accuracies around $ε\sim 10^{-4}$ and we have run it up to $100,000$ atoms. These results outperform current Rydberg atom quantum annealing experimental platforms in both precision and size by orders of magnitude and put severe constraints for future hardware.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a fidelity-per-gate-like metric (accuracy ε for the equation of state) to benchmark quantum annealing quality, rather than just optimization performance. Using two simulated quantum annealing methods (variational QMC up to 100M atoms and Green's function QMC up to 100K atoms), they find classical simulations can achieve ε ~ 10⁻²–10⁻⁴, outperforming current Rydberg atom quantum annealers by orders of magnitude.
AI.motivation: Current benchmarking of quantum annealers focuses on optimization success compared to classical algorithms, which is brittle and problem-dependent. The authors seek a more intrinsic metric that measures the quality of the annealing process itself, analogous to fidelity-per-gate in gate-based quantum computers.
AI.method: The authors introduce an accuracy metric ε for the equation of state of the quantum annealer. They compute benchmark values using two simulated quantum annealing variants for Rydberg atom systems: (1) variational quantum Monte-Carlo with a thermal-annealing-inspired ansatz, and (2) Green's function quantum Monte-Carlo.
AI.result: The variational QMC approach achieves ε ~ 10⁻²–10⁻³ and scales to 100,000,000 atoms on a single CPU. The Green's function QMC reaches ε ~ 10⁻⁴ and scales to 100,000 atoms. Both precision and system size outperform current Rydberg atom quantum annealing experimental platforms by orders of magnitude.
AI.conclusion: Classical simulated annealing methods can achieve high-fidelity quantum annealing for large systems, setting severe constraints on the precision and scale that future quantum annealing hardware must surpass to demonstrate a quantum advantage.

title: Measures of Chirality in Mixed-State Topological Phases
summary: What does it mean for a mixed-state topological phase to be chiral? Mathematically, chirality can be sharply characterized through the symmetry algebra of the mixed state. Physically, however, the question is far more subtle. In pure states, chirality in topological phase is tied to a web of familiar diagnostics, involving bulk-boundary correspondence, a gapless entanglement spectrum, a nontrivial modular commutator, and a quantized thermal Hall response. We show that none of these diagnostics remain reliable in mixed states. Instead, for decohered topological phases with a known error-free parent state, we propose two relative-entropy-based measures that can diagnose chirality, with one of them further extracting the chiral central charge. Our results emphasize how mixed-state topology demands intrinsically new diagnostics beyond direct analogues of pure-state probes.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates chirality in mixed-state topological phases, showing that standard pure-state diagnostics (bulk-boundary correspondence, gapless entanglement spectrum, modular commutator, thermal Hall response) all fail for mixed states. Instead, the authors propose two relative-entropy-based measures that can diagnose chirality and extract the chiral central charge from decohered topological phases.
AI.motivation: Chirality is well-understood in pure-state topological phases via multiple diagnostics, but its definition and detection in mixed-state topological phases (which are more realistic due to decoherence) is unclear and requires fundamentally new approaches.
AI.method: The authors test standard pure-state chirality diagnostics on mixed states and demonstrate their failure. They then introduce two relative-entropy-based measures tailored for decohered topological phases with a known error-free parent state, one of which can extract the chiral central charge.
AI.result: None of the familiar pure-state chirality diagnostics (bulk-boundary correspondence, gapless entanglement spectrum, modular commutator, quantized thermal Hall response) remain reliable for mixed states. The proposed relative-entropy measures successfully diagnose chirality in the mixed-state setting.
AI.conclusion: Mixed-state topology requires intrinsically new diagnostics that go beyond straightforward analogues of pure-state probes; relative-entropy-based measures offer a promising direction for characterizing chirality in decohered topological phases.

title: Permutation asymmetry unlocks emergent advantage in randomized Bell tests
summary: All maximally entangled two-qubit states violate local realism with the same probability under uniformly random projective measurements, yet they need not behave identically in randomized Bell tests. We show that when measurement settings are exchanged between the parties in sequential Bell experiments, permutation symmetry of the shared state determines the statistical relation between the two realizations. Permutationally invariant states yield identical nonlocality outcomes in both experiments, whereas asymmetric states can violate local realism in one realization but not in the other. This distinction leads to two operational consequences. First, it enables the detection of correlations between the measurement choices of Alice and Bob through the joint violation statistics. Second, in Bell tests with finite measurement pools, asymmetric maximally entangled states can significantly increase the probability of observing nonlocality without requiring additional resources. Our results identify permutation asymmetry as a useful feature in randomized Bell experiments and highlight a new role of symmetry in quantum nonlocality.

AI.tldr: Permutation asymmetry in maximally entangled two-qubit states enables distinct nonlocality outcomes in sequential Bell tests with swapped measurement settings, leading to detection of measurement-choice correlations and increased nonlocality probability without extra resources.
AI.motivation: To understand how permutation symmetry/asymmetry of entangled states affects nonlocality in randomized Bell experiments, particularly when measurement settings are exchanged between parties in sequential tests.
AI.method: Theoretical analysis of sequential Bell experiments where measurement settings are swapped between Alice and Bob, comparing permutationally invariant vs. asymmetric maximally entangled two-qubit states via joint violation statistics.
AI.result: Permutationally invariant states yield identical nonlocality outcomes in both realizations, while asymmetric states can violate local realism in one realization but not the other. Asymmetric states can detect correlations between measurement choices and increase nonlocality probability in finite measurement pools.
AI.conclusion: Permutation asymmetry is a useful resource in randomized Bell tests, revealing a new role of symmetry in quantum nonlocality and enabling practical advantages without additional resources.

title: Optimal observables for quantum-enhanced sensing and applications in a Floquet time crystal sensor
summary: In this work, we discuss how to determine and implement feasible optimal observables for a metrology protocol that saturates the quantum Fisher information (QFI) bound. In particular, we focus our study on a simple protocol, namely the method of moments (MoM). We first demonstrate that the symmetric logarithmic derivative (SLD) operator, a Hermitian observable, once implemented in the MoM, saturates the QFI bound. However, the SLD is generally too complex and typically non-local, rendering its direct experimental realization unfeasible. To overcome this limitation, we explore its structure in a specific sensing model - a Floquet time crystal (FTC) acting as an ac field sensor - and show that the SLD can be approximated by substantially simpler observables, such as the bare spin magnetization or a parity observable, for different relevant initial state preparations. We further corroborate our theoretical predictions in a nuclear magnetic resonance system operating as an FTC sensor, employing experimentally motivated parameters to simulate its performance in a state-of-the-art implementation. In general, our results establish a practical route toward near-optimal metrology in FTC sensors, where the inaccessible SLD operator can be replaced by simpler observables while retaining quantum-enhanced sensitivity.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that while the symmetric logarithmic derivative (SLD) operator saturates the quantum Fisher information bound in method-of-moments metrology, it is impractical to implement directly. In a Floquet time crystal sensor, the SLD can be approximated by simple observables like spin magnetization or parity, enabling near-optimal quantum-enhanced sensitivity, validated via NMR simulations.
AI.motivation: To determine feasible optimal observables for saturating the quantum Fisher information bound in method-of-moments metrology, since the theoretically optimal SLD operator is typically too complex and non-local for direct experimental realization.
AI.method: The study analytically demonstrates that the SLD operator saturates the QFI bound in the method of moments. It then explores the SLD structure in a Floquet time crystal ac field sensor model and shows that simpler observables (spin magnetization, parity) can approximate the SLD for different initial states. Numerical simulations with experimentally motivated NMR parameters validate the approach.
AI.result: The SLD operator, when implemented in the method of moments, saturates the QFI bound. In the FTC sensor model, the SLD can be approximated by substantially simpler observables (bare spin magnetization or parity) depending on initial state preparation. Simulations using NMR parameters confirm these theoretical predictions.
AI.conclusion: A practical route toward near-optimal metrology in Floquet time crystal sensors is established: the inaccessible SLD operator can be replaced by simpler observables while retaining quantum-enhanced sensitivity.

title: A Survey of Quantum Programming Languages
summary: Quantum computing has seen multiple recent breakthroughs and is getting closer to demonstrations of an exponential advantage over classical computing for certain problems. Programmers will require high-level, general-purpose, executable programming languages to express quantum solutions clearly and effectively, and the field has already produced a wide variety of such languages. This paper presents a language classification framework and uses it to survey ten popular quantum programming languages. The findings include conceptual and experimental comparisons that result in a list of challenges for future language design.

AI.tldr: This paper surveys ten quantum programming languages using a classification framework, comparing them conceptually and experimentally, and identifying challenges for future language design.
AI.motivation: As quantum computing advances toward demonstrating exponential advantage, programmers need high-level, general-purpose, executable quantum programming languages. The paper aims to classify and compare existing languages to guide future development.
AI.method: The authors develop a language classification framework and apply it to survey ten popular quantum programming languages, performing both conceptual analysis and experimental comparisons.
AI.result: Conceptual and experimental comparisons across ten quantum languages, yielding a categorized analysis of their features and performance.
AI.conclusion: The survey identifies a set of challenges for future quantum programming language design based on the comparative findings.

title: Complex frequency-dependent quadrature squeezing in semiconductor lasers
summary: We present a comprehensive study of quadrature squeezing in a quantum well laser based on a fully quantum Langevin approach. We compute the frequency-resolved squeezing map of the laser field and identify optimal squeezing curves, revealing, for the first time to our knowledge, both frequency-dependent squeezing and complex or hidden squeezing in a semiconductor laser. We further analyse the role of the linewidth enhancement factor (alpha factor) in the emergence of these features. Our results establish semiconductor lasers as a platform for the generation of non-classical light and open new perspectives for their application in quantum communication and sensing.

AI.tldr: This paper theoretically demonstrates quadrature squeezing in quantum well lasers using a fully quantum Langevin approach, revealing frequency-dependent and complex/hidden squeezing, and identifies the linewidth enhancement factor (α-factor) as key to these non-classical features.
AI.motivation: To investigate and demonstrate that semiconductor lasers can generate non-classical light (quadrature squeezing), which was previously unexplored in this context, and to understand the role of the α-factor in enabling such quantum features.
AI.method: Fully quantum Langevin approach to compute frequency-resolved squeezing maps of the laser field; analysis of optimal squeezing curves and the influence of the linewidth enhancement factor.
AI.result: First observation of frequency-dependent squeezing and complex/hidden squeezing in a semiconductor laser; identification of the α-factor's role in these phenomena.
AI.conclusion: Semiconductor lasers can serve as a platform for generating non-classical light, opening new applications in quantum communication and sensing.

title: Mechanisms governing photon-pair generation and emission directionality in quantum metasurfaces
summary: Metasurfaces are emerging as a promising platform for photon-pair generation through spontaneous parametric down-conversion, thanks to their compactness, integrability, and intrinsic multifunctionality, which enables the engineering of complex quantum states. However, their full potential remains only partially exploited because the physical mechanisms governing key properties of the generated photon pairs, such as generation efficiency and emission directionality, are not yet fully understood. As a result, metasurface designs and experimental configurations are often optimized through trial-and-error procedures. Here, we theoretically investigate the main mechanisms that control photon-pair generation and detection by studying how different pump configurations and measurement geometries affect the generation efficiency, emission directionality, and collection efficiency of the emitted photon pairs. This framework allows us to interpret existing experimental results and to provide general guidelines for the design of metasurfaces and the choice of experimental configurations in future experiments. Finally, we show that substrate thickness and multilayer configurations represent additional degrees of freedom for quantum metasurface design and can be engineered to enhance the generation efficiency and control the emission directionality, providing a new route for the optimization of photon-pair sources based on metasurfaces.

AI.tldr: This paper theoretically investigates the physical mechanisms governing photon-pair generation via spontaneous parametric down-conversion in metasurfaces, providing a framework to understand how pump configurations and measurement geometries affect efficiency, directionality, and collection. It also identifies substrate thickness and multilayer configurations as new degrees of freedom for optimizing quantum metasurface designs.
AI.motivation: Metasurfaces hold promise for photon-pair generation but their full potential is underutilized because the physical mechanisms controlling key properties (efficiency, directionality) are not fully understood, leading to trial-and-error optimization.
AI.method: Theoretical investigation of how different pump configurations and measurement geometries influence generation efficiency, emission directionality, and collection efficiency of photon pairs from metasurfaces.
AI.result: A framework that explains existing experimental results and provides design guidelines; additionally, substrate thickness and multilayer configurations are shown to be effective degrees of freedom for enhancing efficiency and controlling directionality.
AI.conclusion: Substrate thickness and multilayer configurations offer new routes for optimizing metasurface-based photon-pair sources, moving beyond trial-and-error toward guided design.

title: Tailor Made Embeddings for Quantum Machine Learning
summary: Autoencoders transformed classical machine learning by solving the curse of dimensionality, enabling principled weight initialization and learning compact, structured representations. In this work, we extend this paradigm to quantum machine learning by introducing a variational autoencoder framework that learns task-specific quantum embeddings of classical data. We demonstrate that high-dimensional datasets, including ImageNet, can be compressed into a 13-qubit quantum representation while remaining reconstructable through a learned decoder. On MNIST (3 vs 5), our approach achieves 98.5% validation accuracy using a circuit-centric quantum classifier, within 1.2 percentage points of a classical neural network baseline (99.7%) and more than 30 percentage points above a naive amplitude-embedding approach. Unlike amplitude embeddings, which require full quantum state tomography for recovery, or angle embeddings, which generally rely on circuit inversion under restrictive assumptions, the proposed framework reconstructs the original data from only a polynomial number of measurements. The framework was further validated on IBM quantum hardware, confirming that the learned embeddings remain stable and reconstructable under real device noise.

AI.tldr: This paper extends variational autoencoders to quantum machine learning, demonstrating that high-dimensional classical data (e.g., ImageNet) can be compressed into a 13-qubit quantum representation and reconstructed from polynomial measurements. On MNIST (3 vs 5), a quantum classifier achieves 98.5% validation accuracy, within 1.2 pp of classical baselines and 30+ pp above naive amplitude embedding. The framework is validated on real IBM quantum hardware under noise.
AI.motivation: To extend the classical autoencoder paradigm—which addresses the curse of dimensionality and learns compact representations—to quantum machine learning by developing a variational autoencoder that learns task-specific quantum embeddings of classical data.
AI.method: The authors introduce a variational autoencoder framework that learns quantum embeddings of classical data, compressing high-dimensional datasets (e.g., ImageNet) into a 13-qubit quantum representation. Reconstruction is achieved via a learned decoder using only a polynomial number of measurements, avoiding full tomography or circuit inversion.
AI.result: On MNIST (3 vs 5), the approach achieves 98.5% validation accuracy with a circuit-centric quantum classifier, within 1.2 percentage points of a classical neural network baseline (99.7%) and >30 percentage points above naive amplitude embedding. The framework is validated on IBM quantum hardware, showing stability under real device noise.
AI.conclusion: The proposed quantum variational autoencoder framework successfully compresses classical data into compact quantum representations that are reconstructable from polynomial measurements, achieves competitive classification performance, and remains robust to noise on real quantum hardware, offering a practical alternative to amplitude and angle embeddings.

title: Improving device-independent quantum key distribution protocols through multiple routed Bell tests
summary: Device-independent quantum key distribution (DI-QKD) offers security with the smallest possible set of assumptions about the experimental setup. The challenge posed by its implementation could be tackled using routed Bell tests with entanglement swapping, or distant Bell state measurement (BSM) units. However, practical distances still require local tests with close-to-ideal violations. We propose a DI-QKD protocol based on multiple sources and measurement devices where, in each round, routed tests are performed on randomly selected local devices. The violation of local Bell tests is checked even when a successful BSM projection is achieved. By requiring that such conditional tests remain consistent with the overall one, we achieve improvements in the critical detection efficiencies of about $4-12\%$ for high visibilities. Our approach enables long-distance DI-QKD, with access to highly efficient loophole-free routing setups, and multiple local tests (possibly imperfect) with very high local detection efficiencies. Finally, we extend the concept of routing to dimension witnesses, where qubit-bounded sources send states to the BSM. This can be seen as a semi-device-independent extension of the aforementioned protocol.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a DI-QKD protocol using multiple sources and measurement devices with routed Bell tests and entanglement swapping, achieving 4-12% improvements in critical detection efficiencies and enabling long-distance security with high-visibility local tests, while also extending routing to dimension witnesses for semi-device-independent security.
AI.motivation: To overcome practical distance limitations in DI-QKD by using routed Bell tests with entanglement swapping and multiple local test devices, while improving critical detection efficiency thresholds.
AI.method: A multi-source, multi-device DI-QKD protocol where routed tests are performed on randomly selected local devices; conditional Bell violations are required to remain consistent even after successful BSM projection; the concept is extended to dimension-witness-based routing for semi-device-independent scenarios.
AI.result: Critical detection efficiencies improved by approximately 4-12% for high visibilities; the protocol enables long-distance DI-QKD with loophole-free routing setups and high local detection efficiencies.
AI.conclusion: The proposed routing-based approach with conditional consistency checks significantly enhances DI-QKD practicality over long distances, and dimension-witness routing offers a semi-device-independent extension.

title: Equivalence of non-local computation tasks beyond Clifford operations
summary: Non-local quantum computation (NLQC) studies how two collaborating players can implement channels on distributed systems using a single simultaneous round of quantum communication and shared entanglement. NLQC has applications in diverse areas, ranging from quantum position-verification to quantum gravity. Recently, it has been realized that the relationships among families of NLQC tasks are highly structured: many seemingly distinct tasks are related by reductions, wherein implementations of one task can be used to efficiently implement a second task. This is analogous to the notion of reduction in complexity theory, and reveals the relative hardness of NLQC tasks. In this work we continue the study of reductions among NLQC tasks. We focus on NLQC examples of the greatest interest in quantum position-verification; in particular examples involving large classical inputs and fixed-size quantum inputs, since these constitute the most feasible protocols for position-verification schemes. Within this setting, we find many new relationships among NLQC tasks. For instance, protocols for the simplest example of redirecting a quantum system based on a classical control imply protocols for controlled single qubit measurements in arbitrary bases, the controlled application of any Clifford unitary, and even the controlled application of any unitary of the form $U=C_1DC_0$ with $D$ an arbitrary diagonal unitary and $C_0, C_1$ Clifford circuits. This implies that many feasible position-verification schemes have the same asymptotic scaling for their entanglement cost, and hence a similar level of security. Our techniques rely on ideas from gate teleportation and measurement based quantum computation, among other areas, bringing several new strategies into NLQC which may be of independent interest.

AI.tldr: This paper studies reductions among non-local quantum computation (NLQC) tasks, particularly those relevant to quantum position-verification. It shows that many seemingly distinct NLQC tasks are related, with protocols for simple tasks implying protocols for more complex ones (e.g., controlled Clifford unitaries and diagonal-unitarily-decomposable gates). This reveals that many position-verification schemes share similar asymptotic entanglement cost and security levels, using techniques from gate teleportation and measurement-based quantum computation.
AI.motivation: To understand the relative hardness of NLQC tasks by establishing reductions among them, analogous to complexity theory reductions, especially for tasks relevant to quantum position-verification with large classical inputs and fixed-size quantum inputs.
AI.method: The authors use reduction techniques to relate different NLQC tasks. They show that protocols for redirecting a quantum system based on classical control can be used to implement controlled single-qubit measurements in arbitrary bases, controlled Clifford unitaries, and controlled unitaries of the form U=C₁ D C₀ (where D is diagonal and C₀, C₁ are Clifford). Techniques are drawn from gate teleportation and measurement-based quantum computation.
AI.result: Many NLQC tasks relevant to quantum position-verification are reducible to each other, implying they share the same asymptotic scaling of entanglement cost and similar security levels. Simple classical-control-based redirecting protocols can enable complex controlled quantum operations.
AI.conclusion: The structured relationships among NLQC tasks reveal that many feasible position-verification schemes have comparable entanglement costs and security, and the new reduction strategies introduced (from gate teleportation and MBQC) may be of independent interest for future NLQC research.

title: Algebraic structures of the Lindblad equation
summary: We investigate the algebraic structure underlying the Lindblad equation for finite-dimensional open quantum systems. By introducing a suitable operator representation of the Liouville superoperator, we show that the dynamics can be formulated in terms of a closed algebra of Hermitian operators that is independent of the particular physical model. This formulation reveals that dissipative dynamics requires a substantially richer algebraic structure than purely unitary evolution, thereby providing a clear characterization of the additional complexity introduced by the Lindbladian. The resulting framework naturally leads to parametrizations of the dynamical map and to differential equations governing its evolution. We further derive recursion relations that enable the efficient construction of the algebra for systems of increasing dimension. Because the algebraic basis is universal, while all model-dependent information enters through a single set of coefficients, the proposed approach significantly reduces the computational cost of constructing the Liouville superoperator compared with direct methods. To facilitate the implementation of the method, we provide a Mathematica notebook containing a one-qubit example that can be systematically extended to an arbitrary number of qubits. The proposed framework therefore provides both a general mathematical description of finite-dimensional Lindblad dynamics and a practical foundation for efficient analytical and numerical implementations.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a universal algebraic framework for the Lindblad equation in finite-dimensional open quantum systems, constructing a closed algebra of Hermitian operators that separates the universal algebraic structure from model-specific coefficients, enabling efficient construction of the Liouville superoperator and providing recursion relations for scalable implementation.
AI.motivation: To characterize the algebraic structure underlying Lindblad dynamics beyond unitary evolution, revealing the additional complexity introduced by dissipative processes and providing a universal mathematical description independent of specific physical models.
AI.method: The authors introduce an operator representation of the Liouville superoperator, formulate the dynamics using a closed algebra of Hermitian operators, derive recursion relations for scalable construction, and provide a Mathematica notebook for implementation.
AI.result: Demonstrates that dissipative dynamics requires a richer algebraic structure than unitary evolution; the universal algebraic basis with model-dependent coefficients significantly reduces computational cost compared to direct methods for constructing the Liouville superoperator.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides both a general mathematical description of finite-dimensional Lindblad dynamics and a practical foundation for efficient analytical and numerical implementations, scalable to arbitrary numbers of qubits.

title: Non-Hermitian Bloch Oscillations
summary: We establish a general framework for non-Hermitian Bloch oscillations by investigating the wave-packet dynamics in one-dimensional non-Hermitian lattices driven by a dc force. The equations of motion for the momentum, center of mass, and group velocity of a wave packet are derived, where an anomalous group velocity due to the non-Hermiticity is identified. We show that nonreciprocal non-smooth Bloch oscillations, characterized by periodic jumps in group velocity, can emerge, and we analyze the role of finite-size effects. In non-Hermitian lattices with unidirectional hopping under open boundary conditions, we further uncover the emergence of periodic temporal Goos--Hänchen shifts together with an anomalous wave propagation along the direction of vanishing hopping.

AI.tldr: A general framework for non-Hermitian Bloch oscillations is developed, revealing anomalous group velocity, nonreciprocal non-smooth oscillations with periodic jumps, finite-size effects, and temporal Goos–Hänchen shifts in unidirectional hopping lattices.
AI.motivation: To establish a general theoretical framework for understanding Bloch oscillations in non-Hermitian systems, where conventional Hermitian approaches fail due to the presence of non-Hermiticity and nonreciprocal hopping.
AI.method: The authors derive equations of motion for momentum, center of mass, and group velocity of wave packets in one-dimensional non-Hermitian lattices under a dc force, analyzing both periodic boundary conditions and open boundary conditions with unidirectional hopping.
AI.result: Identified an anomalous group velocity contribution due to non-Hermiticity; discovered nonreciprocal non-smooth Bloch oscillations with periodic jumps in group velocity; revealed periodic temporal Goos–Hänchen shifts and anomalous wave propagation along the direction of vanishing hopping under open boundary conditions.
AI.conclusion: Non-Hermiticity fundamentally alters Bloch oscillation dynamics, introducing novel phenomena such as anomalous group velocity, non-smooth oscillatory behavior, and temporal Goos–Hänchen shifts, with implications for wave manipulation in non-Hermitian systems.

title: Scattering theory for cavity-assisted spin-motion-photon interactions
summary: Cavity-assisted photon scattering (CAPS) is a powerful mechanism for realizing strong interactions between the internal states of stationary qubits and flying photons, underpinning a broad range of hybrid atom-photon protocols including remote entanglement generation and heralded atom-photon gates. Recently, the motional quantum state has emerged as an important building block for quantum information processing with atomic qubits, both as a coherently controllable degree of freedom and as a fundamental error channel through undesired spin-motion coupling. For the resonant-coupling regime of cavity quantum electrodynamics relevant to CAPS operations, however, the analytical formulation of spin-motion-photon coupling has so far remained elusive. Here, we develop a complete analytical framework for CAPS that incorporates the coherent interaction between atomic motion and a reflected photon by extending scattering theory to include the motional degree of freedom. The resulting compact operator-based input-output relation applies uniformly across various cavity geometries, spin-dependent trapping potentials, and nonidentical multiple spins. As an exemplary application, we use the framework to elucidate how atomic motion affects CAPS-based atom-photon gates, identifying the parameter regimes that suppress motion-induced errors. Our framework provides a theoretical foundation both for mitigating motional errors in CAPS operations and for deliberately exploiting motion-photon interaction at the atom-photon interface.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a complete analytical framework for Cavity-Assisted Photon Scattering (CAPS) that incorporates atomic motion, extending scattering theory to include the motional degree of freedom. This yields a compact operator-based input-output relation applicable across various cavity geometries and trapping potentials, and is used to analyze motion-induced errors in atom-photon gates.
AI.motivation: While CAPS enables strong spin-photon interactions critical for quantum protocols, and atomic motional states are increasingly important in quantum information processing, no analytical formulation existed for spin-motion-photon coupling in the resonant-coupling regime of cavity QED relevant to CAPS.
AI.method: Extension of scattering theory to incorporate the motional degree of freedom of atoms, resulting in a compact operator-based input-output relation that uniformly handles various cavity geometries, spin-dependent trapping potentials, and nonidentical multiple spins.
AI.result: A complete analytical framework for CAPS including coherent spin-motion-photon interactions, with identified parameter regimes that suppress motion-induced errors in atom-photon gates.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a theoretical foundation both for mitigating motional errors in CAPS operations and for deliberately engineering motion-photon interactions at the atom-photon interface.

title: Graph Structures for Local Distinguishability of Quantum Product States
summary: We consider the problem of distinguishing sets of quantum product states with local operations and classical communication (LOCC). Recent work has used graph theory to identify sets of product states distinguishable with one-way LOCC. We extend these efforts to full two-way LOCC, with the first significant analysis of the set of graphs corresponding to bipartite product states that can be distinguished with two-way protocols after finitely many steps. We derive basic closure properties of the set of distinguishable graphs and identify some classes of graphs that guarantee local distinguishability and some graphs that do not. We also include several examples and forward-looking comments.

AI.tldr: This paper extends graph-theoretic analysis from one-way LOCC to two-way LOCC for distinguishing sets of quantum product states, deriving closure properties and identifying classes of graphs that guarantee or preclude local distinguishability.
AI.motivation: Previous work used graph theory to characterize sets of product states distinguishable with one-way LOCC. This paper aims to extend that framework to the more general and practically relevant setting of two-way LOCC communication protocols.
AI.method: The authors analyze the set of graphs corresponding to bipartite product states distinguishable under two-way LOCC protocols with finitely many steps. They derive closure properties of distinguishable graphs and identify graph classes that ensure or prevent local distinguishability.
AI.result: Basic closure properties of the set of distinguishable graphs are established. Specific graph classes that guarantee local distinguishability are identified, along with counterexamples that do not admit such distinguishing protocols.
AI.conclusion: The graph-theoretic approach extends naturally to two-way LOCC, providing new structural insights into which product state sets are locally distinguishable. Examples and future directions are provided.

title: Quantum Fast-Forwarding Beyond Reversibility: The $α$-Perturbed $n$-Cycle
summary:
Quantum fast-forwarding (QFF) is usually formulated for reversible Markov chains, where the projected quantum walk evolution is exactly governed by Chebyshev polynomials of a Hermitian discriminant matrix. We study whether this framework can be extended to nonreversible dynamics for an $α$-perturbed $n$-cycle Markov chain, which preserves circulant structure while introducing controlled irreversibility.
  We show that the nonreversible case has a fundamental obstruction: for $α\neq 0$, the eigenvalues of $P_α$ leave the interval $[-1,1]$, so $T_m(P_α)$ is not uniformly bounded and cannot arise as an exact unitary compression for all times. Thus, exact Chebyshev-based QFF does not extend directly beyond reversibility.
  Nevertheless, we obtain a finite-time approximation result using truncated Chebyshev and LCU techniques. The evolution $P_α^t$ can be approximated with degree $τ=O\left(|α|t+\sqrt{t\log(t/η)}\right),$ which recovers the reversible $O(\sqrt t)$ behavior only in the perturbative regime $|α|=O(t^{-1/2})$. This identifies a nearly reversible regime where QFF survives perturbatively and quantifies how irreversibility degrades the speedup.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether Quantum Fast-Forwarding (QFF), originally designed for reversible Markov chains, can be extended to nonreversible dynamics using an α-perturbed n-cycle Markov chain. It shows that exact Chebyshev-based QFF fails for nonreversible cases because eigenvalues of P_α leave [-1,1], but a finite-time approximation is possible using truncated Chebyshev and LCU techniques, with degree scaling of O(|α|t + √(t log(t/η))). The reversible O(√t) speedup survives only in the perturbative regime |α| = O(t^{-1/2}).
AI.motivation: To examine whether quantum fast-forwarding (QFF) can be extended from reversible to nonreversible Markov chains, by studying an α-perturbed n-cycle as a testing ground for controlled irreversibility.
AI.method: Analytical eigenvalue analysis of the perturbed circulant Markov chain P_α; application of truncated Chebyshev polynomials and LCU (Linear Combination of Unitaries) to approximate P_α^t; derivation of the degree bound τ = O(|α|t + √(t log(t/η))).
AI.result: Exact Chebyshev-based QFF breaks down for α ≠ 0 due to eigenvalues leaving [-1,1]. However, a finite-time approximation exists, achieving O(√t) scaling only when |α| = O(t^{-1/2}) (nearly reversible regime), with irreversibility linearly degrading the speedup.
AI.conclusion: Exact QFF does not extend beyond reversible dynamics, but perturbative QFF survives in a nearly reversible regime, with the degree of the approximation capturing how irreversibility degrades the quantum speedup.

title: Non-Hermiticity of an anomalous superradiant phase
summary: We counterintuitively present a Hermitian squeezing-Dicke model as a minimal setting for non-Hermitian physics in many-body light-matter systems. It enables the realization of a non-Hermitian Hamiltonian of interest using a Hermitian quadratic bosonic system. Unlike previous dissipation-driven non-Hermitian mechanisms, effective parity-time ($\mathcal{PT}$) symmetry arises purely from squeezing and exchanges gainy and lossy eigenmodes. We identify non-Hermiticity of an anomalous superradiant phase for strong spins squeezing, exhibiting spontaneous breaking of the unique $\mathcal{PT}$ symmetry beyond $Z_2$ symmetries. Such exotic phase exhibits a complex excitation spectrum and undergoes a dynamical phase transition to a conventional superradiant phase at an exceptional point. An artificial magnetic field combined with the broken Hermiticity yields nonreciprocal dynamics with striking quantum amplification, exhibiting unidirectional enhanced transmission. Our Hermitian light-matter system offers an alternative pathway to exotic non-Hermitian physics and nonreciprocal quantum amplification.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a Hermitian squeezing-Dicke model that generates non-Hermitian physics (PT-symmetry, exceptional points, nonreciprocal amplification) purely through bosonic squeezing interactions without actual dissipation.
AI.motivation: To realize non-Hermitian physics (PT-symmetry, exceptional points) in a fully Hermitian many-body light-matter system, avoiding the need for actual gain/loss dissipation mechanisms.
AI.method: A Hermitian squeezing-Dicke model with quadratic bosonic interactions that mimics a non-Hermitian Hamiltonian; effective PT-symmetry arises from squeezing rather than dissipation; analysis of anomalous superradiant phase and its complex excitation spectrum.
AI.result: Identification of an anomalous superradiant phase with broken PT-symmetry beyond Z2 symmetries, exhibiting complex spectrum and an exceptional point; realization of nonreciprocal dynamics with unidirectional quantum amplification under an artificial magnetic field.
AI.conclusion: Hermitian light-matter systems can serve as an alternative platform for exploring exotic non-Hermitian physics and achieving nonreciprocal quantum amplification.

title: Nonadiabatic Holonomic Single-Qubit Gates in Non-Hermitian Systems
summary: Holonomic quantum computation offers a promising route to robust quantum gates, but decoherence remains a central obstacle in realistic implementations. Here we develop a nonadiabatic holonomic scheme for a driven three-level system in the no-jump regime described by an effective non-Hermitian Hamiltonian. Within a biorthogonal framework, tailored complex pulses enforce exact closure of the computational-subspace evolution at the final time despite the underlying nonunitary dynamics, enabling arbitrary single-qubit holonomic gates without requiring cyclic evolution in its orthogonal complement. In contrast to existing non-Hermitian treatments, which either neglect the overall exponential prefactor or, in adiabatic settings, include dissipation only on the auxiliary excited level, our scheme incorporates decay and dephasing of all bare eigenstates directly into the pulse design, so that dissipation does not reduce the no-jump gate fidelity.

AI.tldr: A nonadiabatic holonomic scheme using a non-Hermitian Hamiltonian is developed for a driven three-level system in the no-jump regime, where tailored complex pulses enforce exact closure of the computational-subspace evolution despite nonunitary dynamics, enabling arbitrary single-qubit holonomic gates without cyclic evolution in the orthogonal complement. The scheme incorporates decay and dephasing of all bare eigenstates directly into pulse design, preventing dissipation from reducing no-jump gate fidelity.
AI.motivation: Decoherence remains a central obstacle in realistic implementations of holonomic quantum computation, motivating the development of a scheme that directly incorporates dissipation into pulse design to maintain gate fidelity.
AI.method: A nonadiabatic holonomic scheme within a biorthogonal framework for a driven three-level system described by an effective non-Hermitian Hamiltonian in the no-jump regime, using tailored complex pulses to enforce exact closure of the computational-subspace evolution at the final time.
AI.result: Arbitrary single-qubit holonomic gates are achievable without requiring cyclic evolution in the orthogonal complement; dissipation of all bare eigenstates (decay and dephasing) is incorporated directly into pulse design, so dissipation does not reduce the no-jump gate fidelity.
AI.conclusion: The proposed nonadiabatic holonomic scheme overcomes decoherence limitations in non-Hermitian treatments by incorporating decay and dephasing of all eigenstates into pulse design, preserving no-jump gate fidelity and enabling robust single-qubit gates.

title: Dissipation-Induced Deviations from Kibble-Zurek Scaling in Non-Hermitian Quantum Annealing
summary: We revisit the quantum annealing problem in the non-Hermitian transverse-field Ising model. We determine, both analytically and numerically, the intrinsic transition probabilities and the resulting defect density. Our results reveal that, unlike the Hermitian case where defect production is dominated by modes near the gap-closing point, the non-Hermitian dynamics involve significant contributions from broad momentum sectors. We find that, depending on the dissipation strength, the defect density exhibits standard Kibble-Zurek scaling, anti-Kibble-Zurek behavior, and a suppression faster than the Kibble-Zurek prediction. We demonstrate that these deviations from the standard Kibble-Zurek scaling can be understood in terms of the underlying excitation probabilities. Specifically, the fast decay of the defect density originates from a vanishing excitation probability spanning a range of annealing times across all allowed modes, even at the gap-closing points. In contrast, the anti-Kibble-Zurek behavior arises from supplementary excitations facilitated by dissipation over a broad range of allowed modes, particularly those situated away from the gap-closing region.

AI.tldr: This paper studies quantum annealing in a non-Hermitian transverse-field Ising model, finding that defect production deviates from standard Kibble-Zurek scaling: it can exhibit standard, anti-Kibble-Zurek, or faster-than-Kibble-Zurek behavior depending on dissipation strength, due to broad momentum sector contributions and dissipation-induced excitation dynamics.
AI.motivation: To understand how non-Hermiticity (dissipation) alters defect production during quantum annealing, moving beyond the Hermitian paradigm where defects are dominated by gap-closing modes.
AI.method: Analytical and numerical analysis of intrinsic transition probabilities and defect density in the non-Hermitian transverse-field Ising model.
AI.result: Defect density shows three regimes depending on dissipation strength: standard Kibble-Zurek scaling, anti-Kibble-Zurek behavior, and suppression faster than Kibble-Zurek prediction. The fast decay originates from vanishing excitation probability across all allowed modes, while anti-Kibble-Zurek arises from dissipation-induced excitations in broad momentum sectors away from the gap-closing region.
AI.conclusion: Non-Hermitian dynamics qualitatively change defect production in quantum annealing, with dissipation enabling both suppression and enhancement of defects beyond the standard Kibble-Zurek framework.

title: Scalable Message-Passing Quantum Graph Neural Networks in the Weisfeiler-Leman Hierarchy
comment: 10 pages, 4 figures (main text); 35 pages, 9 figures, 14 tables including Supplementary Information. Code available at https://github.com/SnehalRaj/mp-qgnns
summary: Graphs provide a natural language for relational data in chemistry, biology and optimisation. Graph neural networks (GNNs) have driven much of the recent progress in learning from such data through message passing, a single primitive that generalises convolution and attention. Quantum counterparts have been proposed, but with limited connection to message passing and few guarantees on performance or scalability. More broadly, the trainability of variational quantum circuits is a recognised bottleneck for their wide applicability, and pre-training has emerged as one way to address it. Yet for a quantum model to be useful, it must offer expressivity guarantees along with demonstrable scalability. Here we show how a quantum graph neural network can be built to perform message passing, to be permutation equivariant, and to sit at a chosen level of the Weisfeiler-Leman hierarchy, the standard measure of how finely a model can tell graphs apart. We show that, as for classical GNNs, the training can be done first on small graph instances, allowing for a pre-training that can mitigate usual training issues, and its output can be read out at a cost that stays low as the graph grows. We validate the framework in large-scale simulations of up to 56 qubits across three datasets, on synthetic graphs that ordinary message passing cannot separate, on molecular property prediction, and on the travelling salesperson problem. Our framework opens a path for near-term quantum algorithms with theoretical guarantees and practical scalability, bringing the principles of graph learning into quantum circuit design.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a quantum graph neural network (QGNN) that performs message passing with permutation equivariance, can be placed at a chosen level of the Weisfeiler-Leman hierarchy, supports pre-training on small graphs to mitigate training issues, and maintains low readout cost as graph size grows. The framework is validated on up to 56 qubits across three datasets: synthetic WL-separability graphs, molecular property prediction, and the travelling salesperson problem.
AI.motivation: Existing quantum counterparts to graph neural networks have limited connection to message passing and lack guarantees on performance or scalability. Additionally, variational quantum circuits suffer from trainability bottlenecks, and pre-training has emerged as a potential remedy.
AI.method: The authors construct a quantum graph neural network that implements message passing, enforces permutation equivariance, and operates at a chosen level of the Weisfeiler-Leman hierarchy. Training is performed first on small graphs as a pre-training strategy to mitigate training issues, and readout cost remains low as the graph scales.
AI.result: Large-scale simulations of up to 56 qubits across three datasets (synthetic WL-indistinguishable graphs, molecular property prediction, TSP) demonstrate the framework's effectiveness.
AI.conclusion: The framework opens a path for near-term quantum algorithms with theoretical guarantees and practical scalability, bringing graph learning principles into quantum circuit design.

title: Shallow Quantum Circuits for Deep Chemistry via Valence Bond Embeddings
summary: Quantum chemistry is one of the major potential applications in quantum computation. Currently there is a considerable focus on relatively small active spaces as a consequence of hardware noise and exponential bottlenecks in simulations. In the long run, there will be an increasing demand in reliable approximations for larger systems -- both, as initial states for projective algorithms like the quantum phase estimation or for the evaluation of dynamical properties. While numerous approaches to select active spaces and extrapolate basis set accuracy exist, there is currently no consistent approach that results in a single quantum circuit for the total system. In this work, we combine hybrid Fermionic-Bosonic encodings with the structured approach of Quantum Valence Bond Theory to directly construct quantum circuits for comparably large molecular systems. With this approach we are able to push simulability barrier of variational quantum eigensolvers towards chemically relevant systems and demonstrate circuit designs that outperform active space counterparts and achieve good approximations with respect to the exact solutions.

AI.tldr: This work combines hybrid Fermionic-Bosonic encodings with Quantum Valence Bond Theory to construct quantum circuits for large molecular systems, pushing the simulability barrier of variational quantum eigensolvers toward chemically relevant systems and outperforming active space approaches.
AI.motivation: Current quantum chemistry simulations face limitations from hardware noise and exponential bottlenecks, restricting them to small active spaces. There is a growing need for reliable approximations for larger systems, both as initial states for projective algorithms like quantum phase estimation and for evaluating dynamical properties.
AI.method: The authors combine hybrid Fermionic-Bosonic encodings with the structured approach of Quantum Valence Bond Theory to directly construct quantum circuits for comparably large molecular systems.
AI.result: The approach pushes the simulability barrier of variational quantum eigensolvers toward chemically relevant systems, and the circuit designs outperform active space counterparts while achieving good approximations to exact solutions.
AI.conclusion: This method provides a consistent approach that results in a single quantum circuit for the total system, addressing the current lack of such a framework for scaling quantum chemistry simulations to larger molecular systems.

title: An ultralow-loss integrated photonic platform for discrete-variable quantum information processing
summary: Photonic integrated circuits offer a scalable and robust route toward quantum information technologies by consolidating photon sources and linear optical networks onto compact, wafer-manufacturable chips. Although silicon photonics has enabled diverse discrete-variable quantum breakthroughs -- spanning multiphoton entanglement, quantum networking, and photonic qubit fusion for quantum computing -- scaling these platforms beyond proof-of-principle demonstrations remains severely constrained by a critical system-level bottleneck. Optical loss compounds rapidly across photon generation, routing, and state analysis, causing multiphoton generation probabilities to plummet exponentially as circuit depth and complexity grow. Here we overcome this rate-loss barrier by demonstrating a monolithic, ultralow-loss silicon nitride (Si$_3$N$_4$) integrated photonic platform engineered for high-performance discrete-variable quantum information processing. Our architecture seamlessly integrates narrowband photon-pair sources with low-loss qubit-fusion circuits and reconfigurable state-analysis interferometers. The on-chip sources prepare Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen (EPR) states with a fidelity of 0.9875(3) and exhibit near-unity photon indistinguishability, yielding a heralded Hong-Ou-Mandel interference visibility of 0.990(6). By executing on-chip fusion of two EPR states, we synthesize and characterize four-photon Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger states with a record fidelity of 0.943(8) and a fourfold count rate of 27 Hz -- more than two orders of magnitude higher than previous silicon-photonic implementations. Combined with standard CMOS-compatible fabrication on 150-mm-diameter wafers, these results establish ultralow-loss Si$_3$N$_4$ integrated photonics as a definitive, manufacturable platform for deployable, large-scale quantum information processors.

AI.tldr: Ultralow-loss silicon nitride (Si₃N₄) integrated photonic platform overcomes optical loss barriers in quantum information processing, demonstrating near-unity photon indistinguishability, record 0.943(8) fidelity four-photon GHZ states with a 27 Hz fourfold count rate (>100× improvement over silicon photonics), and CMOS-compatible manufacturability.
AI.motivation: Optical loss in silicon photonic integrated circuits causes multiphoton generation probabilities to plummet exponentially with circuit depth and complexity, severely constraining scaling beyond proof-of-principle quantum demonstrations. The paper aims to overcome this rate-loss barrier.
AI.method: A monolithic, ultralow-loss Si₃N₄ integrated photonic platform engineered with narrowband photon-pair sources, low-loss qubit-fusion circuits, and reconfigurable state-analysis interferometers, fabricated using standard CMOS-compatible processes on 150-mm wafers.
AI.result: EPR state fidelity of 0.9875(3), near-unity photon indistinguishability with heralded HOM interference visibility of 0.990(6), four-photon GHZ state fidelity of 0.943(8) at a fourfold count rate of 27 Hz — over two orders of magnitude higher than prior silicon photonic implementations.
AI.conclusion: Ultralow-loss Si₃N₄ integrated photonics is established as a definitive, manufacturable platform for deployable, large-scale quantum information processors.

title: On the simple derivation of the Casimir effect
summary: The Casimir effect in its simplest form describes the attraction of two parallel conducting plates at close distance due to the vacuum fluctuation of the electromagnetic field. Its derivation can be found in many introductory works on quantum optics. Here we return to the original paper by Casimir and find subtle nuances in his derivation that are worth discussing to give a complete picture of a mathematically sound derivation of the effect.

AI.tldr: This paper re-examines Casimir's original derivation of the Casimir effect, identifying subtle nuances and providing a mathematically rigorous treatment of the attraction between parallel conducting plates due to vacuum fluctuations.
AI.motivation: To revisit Casimir's original derivation and highlight subtle mathematical nuances that are often overlooked, in order to present a complete and mathematically sound derivation of the Casimir effect.
AI.method: The authors return to Casimir's original paper, analyze the derivation step-by-step, and identify subtle nuances that require discussion for a complete mathematical picture.
AI.result: Identification of subtle nuances in Casimir's original derivation that are worth discussing to fully understand the mathematically sound derivation of the effect.
AI.conclusion: A complete and mathematically rigorous derivation of the Casimir effect requires careful attention to subtle nuances present in Casimir's original work, which are often glossed over in introductory treatments.

title: Lattice patch structure for fixed-frequency transmon quantum computer with high-fidelity CNOT gates
summary: Superconducting transmon processors represent a leading platform for large-scale quantum computing due to their high gate fidelities and scalability. However, conventional qubit-coupler-qubit (QCQ) architectures face critical physical and structural bottlenecks, notably frequency crowding [spectator qubit collisions] during system scaling and inefficient mapping onto the standard surface code.To overcome these limitations, we propose a novel lattice-patch architecture that couples four fixed-frequency transmons to a single fixed-frequency coupler.This design enhances qubit connectivity and maps directly onto the surface-code lattice unit [plaquette], thereby minimizing the compilation overhead associated with logical qubit implementation. Furthermore, utilizing an entirely fixed-frequency design intrinsically eliminates susceptibility to external flux noise, ensuring robust operational stability.Multi-level numerical simulations demonstrate CNOT gate fidelities exceeding 0.98 across all six connectivity directions within the patch. Nevertheless, the complex interaction network of the four-qubit architecture induces unintended residual phase accumulation during cross-resonance driving. This parasitic effect necessitates precise calibration, achievable via virtual $R_z$ gates [software phase updates]. Ultimately, our results establish the lattice-patch architecture as an efficient, robust building block for future fault-tolerant quantum computers.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a lattice-patch architecture coupling four fixed-frequency transmons to a single fixed-frequency coupler, replacing conventional qubit-coupler-qubit designs to mitigate frequency crowding and improve surface code mapping. Numerical simulations show CNOT fidelities >0.98, with residual phase effects correctable via virtual Rz gates.
AI.motivation: Conventional qubit-coupler-qubit (QCQ) architectures suffer from frequency crowding and spectator qubit collisions during scaling, and map inefficiently onto the surface code, motivating a new design.
AI.method: A lattice-patch architecture coupling four fixed-frequency transmons to a single fixed-frequency coupler is proposed, with entirely fixed-frequency design to eliminate flux noise. Multi-level numerical simulations and cross-resonance driving are used for characterization.
AI.result: CNOT gate fidelities exceeding 0.98 are achieved across all six connectivity directions in the patch. Residual phase accumulation from the four-qubit interaction network is identified and corrected via virtual Rz gates.
AI.conclusion: The lattice-patch architecture serves as an efficient, robust building block for fault-tolerant quantum computing, addressing key scalability issues in superconducting transmon processors.

title: Witness expansion: A unified framework for analytical and measurable mixed-state resource detection
comment: 19+58 pages, 2 figures, comments are very welcome!
summary: Quantum information science aims to harness different kinds of quantum resources to accomplish specific information-processing tasks. These resources also play an increasingly important role in addressing fundamental questions concerning quantum phases and dynamics. Therefore, developing powerful and practical methods for identifying and detecting quantum resources is of great significance, with applications ranging from benchmarking quantum devices to understanding the fundamental structure of quantum theory. In this work, we propose witness expansion, a unified framework for constructing nonlinear criteria for detecting quantum resources that are associated with a well-defined group of free unitaries. These criteria apply to both pure and mixed quantum states and are based on polynomial functions of the target state, which can be estimated experimentally using multiple copies of the state and evaluated analytically in certain physical models. We show how several well-known resource-detection quantities naturally emerge from our framework, including the $l_2$ norm of coherence, partial-transpose moments for entanglement, stabilizer entropy for nonstabilizerness (quantum magic), and fermionic antiflatness for fermionic non-Gaussianity. Beyond recovering these existing structures, our framework also yields new criteria for detecting qubit and qudit magic states, substantially enhancing witness-based detection capabilities. In addition, it gives, to the best of our knowledge, the first analytical criterion for detecting mixed-state fermionic non-Gaussianity with respect to the convex hull of pure fermionic Gaussian states that remains nontrivial for arbitrary numbers of qubits, demonstrating the broad applicability and conceptual unifying power of the framework.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces "witness expansion," a unified framework for constructing nonlinear criteria to detect various quantum resources (coherence, entanglement, magic, fermionic non-Gaussianity) associated with free unitaries, recovering known detection quantities and producing new criteria, including the first analytical criterion for mixed-state fermionic non-Gaussianity.
AI.motivation: To develop a powerful and practical unified framework for identifying and detecting quantum resources, which is important for benchmarking quantum devices and understanding the structure of quantum theory.
AI.method: Proposes "witness expansion," a unified framework that constructs nonlinear criteria based on polynomial functions of the target state, associated with a well-defined group of free unitaries, applicable to both pure and mixed states and estimable experimentally via multiple copies.
AI.result: The framework recovers known detection quantities (l2 norm of coherence, partial-transpose moments for entanglement, stabilizer entropy for magic, fermionic antiflatness) and yields new criteria for detecting qubit and qudit magic states, plus the first analytical criterion for mixed-state fermionic non-Gaussianity.
AI.conclusion: The witness expansion framework demonstrates broad applicability and conceptual unifying power for detecting diverse quantum resources, including providing novel criteria that substantially enhance detection capabilities.

title: Efficient foundation decoders for fault-tolerant quantum computing
summary: Foundation decoders, a class of high-capacity neural decoders, are leading candidates for fault-tolerant quantum computing, with accurate and efficient decoding at large code distances. However, their construction often faces a steep scaling barrier, as larger code distances rapidly amplify the cost of syndrome generation and neural optimization. To address this bottleneck, here we devise neural transfer unification (NTU), a unified framework for efficient foundation decoders. A central feature of NTU is its ability to align decoding tasks across code distances via algebraic structures shared by scalable code families, which enables knowledge learned on smaller codes to accelerate large-scale decoder training. We instantiate NTU as NTU-Transformer, a transformer-based neural decoder tailored for planar surface codes and bivariate bicycle codes. For planar surface codes under circuit-level noise, NTU-Transformer outperforms correlation-aware matching on the $[\![361,1,19]\!]$ code and further scales to the $[\![625,1,25]\!]$ code, where it exceeds standard matching through transfer adaptation. For the bivariate bicycle code with $[\![72,12,6]\!]$, it surpasses Relay-BP in the low-physical-error regime. These results establish our proposal as a scalable route to amortized cross-distance training of foundation decoders for fault-tolerant quantum processors.

AI.tldr: NTU-Transformer is a neural decoder that uses transfer learning across code distances to enable scalable training for fault-tolerant quantum computing, outperforming existing methods on planar surface codes and bivariate bicycle codes.
AI.motivation: Foundation decoders face a steep scaling barrier where larger code distances dramatically increase the cost of syndrome generation and neural optimization, hindering their practical deployment for fault-tolerant quantum computing.
AI.method: Neural transfer unification (NTU) aligns decoding tasks across different code distances using algebraic structures shared by scalable code families, enabling knowledge transfer from smaller codes to accelerate large-scale decoder training. NTU-Transformer implements this as a transformer-based decoder for planar surface codes and bivariate bicycle codes.
AI.result: NTU-Transformer outperforms correlation-aware matching on the [361,1,19] planar surface code, scales to [625,1,25] via transfer adaptation, and surpasses Relay-BP on the [72,12,6] bivariate bicycle code in the low-physical-error regime.
AI.conclusion: NTU establishes a scalable route to amortized cross-distance training of foundation decoders for fault-tolerant quantum processors.

title: Rate-2/3 Girth-8 (3,18)-Regular Quantum LDPC Codes from Two-Branch Finite-Field Bases and CPM Lifts
summary: We construct a rate-$2/3$ quantum low-density parity-check (LDPC) code from a $(3,18)$-regular two-branch finite-field base and a circulant-permutation-matrix (CPM) lift of degree $P=101$. The resulting code is a Calderbank-Shor-Steane (CSS) code with parameters $[[34542,23032,d\le 310]]$. We do not regard this upper bound as an estimate of the true minimum distance; rather, $d\le310$ is the tightest upper bound currently obtained from structural lifts and decoder-produced logical errors. The construction has row weight 18 and column weight 3, and the Tanner graphs of $H_X$ and $H_Z$ separately have girth 8.
