Decoder experiments with log-likelihood-ratio (LLR) joint belief propagation (BP) and deterministic post-processing show no failures in $10^8$ trials at $p=0.01$, and a finite-length frame error rate (FER) sweep estimates the transition near $p=0.029$.

AI.tldr: A rate-2/3 [[34542,23032,d≤310]] quantum LDPC code from a (3,18)-regular two-branch base with CPM lift (P=101) yields CSS construction, girth 8 Tanner graphs, and decoder experiments showing no failures in 10^8 trials at p=0.01 with FER transition near p=0.029.
AI.motivation: To construct a high-rate quantum LDPC code with practical finite-length performance, achieving a rate-2/3 CSS code with good decoding thresholds and large distance upper bound, addressing the need for efficient quantum error correction codes.
AI.method: Using a (3,18)-regular two-branch finite-field base and a circulant-permutation-matrix (CPM) lift of degree P=101 to construct a CSS code; evaluating via LLR joint belief propagation with deterministic post-processing and finite-length FER sweeps.
AI.result: Parameters [[34542,23032,d≤310]], row weight 18, column weight 3, girth 8 for both H_X and H_Z Tanner graphs; no decoder failures in 10^8 trials at p=0.01, FER transition estimated near p=0.029.
AI.conclusion: The constructed quantum LDPC code demonstrates strong practical performance with high threshold and large distance, though the distance bound d≤310 is from structural lifts and decoder logical errors rather than true minimum distance estimation.

title: Loss-aware pulse sequence optimization for generating photonic Fock states
summary: We investigate the preparation of frequency-tunable photonic Fock states in a hybrid cavity system consisting of a nonlinear medium and a two-level system. Employing a gradient-based optimization approach, we construct multipulse driving protocols that control the system dynamics through pulse amplitudes, phases, and inter-pulse delays. Assuming unitary dynamics, the optimized sequences enable near-deterministic preparation of low-photon-number Fock states. We extend the optimization framework to open-system dynamics by modeling atomic decay and photon loss within the Lindblad master equation. This allows us to identify pulse sequences that exhibit enhanced robustness against dissipation compared to those optimized under idealized assumptions. Furthermore, we find that optimal pulse sequences obey strict constraints on relative phases, which are limited to values of 0 or $π$. These phase restrictions are supported by an analytical study that investigates a simple two-pulse sequence treating the second pulse perturbatively.

AI.tldr: The paper develops optimized multipulse driving protocols for preparing frequency-tunable photonic Fock states in a hybrid cavity system (nonlinear medium + two-level system), achieving near-deterministic low-photon-number state preparation under unitary dynamics and enhanced robustness against dissipation when optimized under open-system conditions, with optimal phases constrained to 0 or π.
AI.motivation: To achieve frequency-tunable photonic Fock state preparation in a hybrid cavity system with enhanced robustness against dissipation, addressing the challenge of generating non-classical light states in realistic open quantum systems.
AI.method: Gradient-based optimization to construct multipulse driving protocols controlling pulse amplitudes, phases, and inter-pulse delays; Lindblad master equation for open-system dynamics modeling atomic decay and photon loss; perturbative analytical study of two-pulse sequences to explain phase restrictions.
AI.result: Near-deterministic preparation of low-photon-number Fock states under unitary dynamics; enhanced robustness against dissipation when optimized under open-system conditions; optimal pulse phases strictly constrained to 0 or π.
AI.conclusion: Open-system optimization yields more robust pulse sequences than unitary-only optimization, and optimal phases are limited to 0 or π, consistent with analytical perturbative analysis.

title: From Approximate Floquet Engineering to Full Floquet Theory: Coherent Control of Chiral Spin Systems in Spintronics
summary: Coherent control of interacting spin systems under time-periodic driving is a central challenge in spin-based quantum technologies. Here we demonstrate the applicability of a full Floquet-space formalism, adapted from Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) methodologies, to model the dynamics of driven coupled electron spins in the presence of a static magnetic field B0 and a transverse oscillating field B1. The framework explicitly includes isotropic exchange coupling J and the chiral Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya antisymmetric exchange interaction (DMI), and its numerical convergence is systematically validated with respect to Fourier-space truncation. In the non-interacting limit, the expected driven-spin dynamics is recovered, with the oscillation periodicity governed by B1. Exchange coupling alone does not modify the collective spin expectation values under the chosen initial condition, consistent with symmetry considerations. In contrast, increasing DMI generates a finite expectation value of Sy, suppresses the expectation value of Sz, and produces tilted, elliptical Bloch-sphere trajectories, reflecting the emergence of chiral spin-spin correlations. These effects are pronounced for open boundary conditions, while remaining nearly negligible in the periodic boundary case. When exchange coupling and DMI coexist, the dynamics becomes strongly perturbed and multi-frequency in nature. Together, these results demonstrate that full Floquet-space modeling provides a robust and predictive framework for analyzing and engineering coherent dynamics in driven interacting spin systems beyond simple coherent-rotation regimes.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates a full Floquet-space formalism, adapted from NMR, to model driven coupled electron spins with exchange coupling (J) and Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction (DMI). DMI induces chiral spin correlations and elliptical Bloch-sphere trajectories, while coexistence with exchange produces multi-frequency dynamics. The framework shows robust predictive power beyond simple coherent-rotation regimes.
AI.motivation: Coherent control of interacting spin systems under time-periodic driving is a central challenge in spin-based quantum technologies, and existing models often fail to capture the full complexity of driven dynamics beyond simple coherent-rotation regimes.
AI.method: A full Floquet-space formalism adapted from NMR methodologies is applied, explicitly including isotropic exchange coupling J and chiral Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya antisymmetric exchange interaction (DMI). The framework's numerical convergence is systematically validated with respect to Fourier-space truncation, and dynamics are studied under open vs. periodic boundary conditions.
AI.result: In the non-interacting limit, driven-spin dynamics with B1-periodicity are recovered. Exchange coupling alone does not modify collective spin expectation values. Increasing DMI generates finite ⟨Sy⟩, suppresses ⟨Sz⟩, and produces tilted elliptical Bloch-sphere trajectories. These effects are pronounced for open boundary conditions but nearly negligible for periodic boundaries. Coexisting J and DMI produce strongly perturbed multi-frequency dynamics.
AI.conclusion: Full Floquet-space modeling provides a robust and predictive framework for analyzing and engineering coherent dynamics in driven interacting spin systems beyond simple coherent-rotation regimes.

title: Quantum group codes for non-Clifford logic: enhanced decoding, addressability and parallelizability
summary: We introduce a framework based on classical quasi group codes to define a class of quantum CSS codes, called quantum group codes, supporting transversal multi-control-$Z$ gates which are both addressable and parallelizable, thus allowing to efficiently implement circuits composed of non-Clifford gates at the logical level. Building on this, we use a lifting procedure of classical AG codes established from class field theory to construct good quantum group codes with improved decoding complexity and logical multi-control-$Z$ gate parallelizability. More precisely, on input a good quantum AG code over the alphabet $\mathbb F_q$ with transversal $\mathsf{C}^m\mathsf Z$ gate, we apply this lifting procedure to its underlying classical AG code and obtain a quantum group code over the alphabet $\mathbb F_{q^2}$ supporting a transversal $\mathsf{C}^m\mathsf Z$ gate as well as addressable and parallelizable $\mathsf{C}^{m-1}\mathsf Z$ gates. In addition, this quantum code admits a quasi-quadratic time decoder with a linear decoding radius. This is to be compared with the previous quantum AG codes which have a cubic-time decoder. Hence, our work implies a decrease of the time complexity of state-of-the-art magic-state distillation protocols by an almost linear factor.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces quantum group codes based on classical quasi group codes, enabling transversal, addressable, and parallelizable multi-control-Z gates. Using a lifting procedure from classical AG codes via class field theory, they construct good quantum group codes with quasi-quadratic time decoding (vs. cubic for prior AG codes) and linear decoding radius, improving magic-state distillation protocols by an almost linear factor.
AI.motivation: To improve the efficiency of non-Clifford gate implementation at the logical level in quantum error-correcting codes, particularly by enabling addressable and parallelizable transversal multi-control-Z gates while reducing decoding complexity.
AI.method: The authors define quantum group codes from classical quasi group codes, then apply a lifting procedure of classical AG codes (established from class field theory) to construct quantum group codes over F_{q^2} that support transversal C^m Z gates and addressable/parallelizable C^{m-1}Z gates.
AI.result: The constructed quantum codes admit a quasi-quadratic time decoder with a linear decoding radius, compared to previous quantum AG codes requiring cubic-time decoders. This implies an almost linear factor speedup in magic-state distillation protocols.
AI.conclusion: The work demonstrates that quantum group codes offer a practical improvement over prior quantum AG codes by reducing decoding complexity and enhancing gate parallelism, leading to more efficient fault-tolerant quantum computation.

title: A 0.651-approximation to quantum Max Cut via Rydberg atoms
summary: Quantum Max Cut, also known as the anti-ferromagnetic Heisenberg Hamiltonian, is a QMA-complete problem which serves as a benchmark for approximation algorithms in quantum physics. Here we develop a hybrid approximation algorithm to quantum Max Cut, which uses the natural quantum dynamics of Rydberg atom systems in combination with semidefinite programming and randomized rounding. It achieves a conditional approximation ratio of $0.651$, compared to the best-known ratio of $0.614$ that relies on semidefinite programming alone. The algorithm is robust in the sense that the advantage persists even if the annealing procedure of the Rydberg atom system obtains a state whose energy is only $89\%$ of its true ground state energy. Our approach opens a new route for hybrid quantum-classical algorithms that combine quantum with classical optimization methods.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a hybrid quantum-classical algorithm for Quantum Max Cut that combines Rydberg atom dynamics with semidefinite programming and randomized rounding, achieving an improved approximation ratio of 0.651 (vs. 0.614 for SDP alone).
AI.motivation: Quantum Max Cut (anti-ferromagnetic Heisenberg Hamiltonian) is QMA-complete and serves as a benchmark for approximation algorithms in quantum physics. The goal is to improve upon the best-known approximation ratio of 0.614 achieved by semidefinite programming alone.
AI.method: The hybrid algorithm combines natural quantum dynamics of Rydberg atom systems with semidefinite programming and randomized rounding. The quantum annealing procedure of the Rydberg system is used as a component within the classical optimization pipeline.
AI.result: Achieves a conditional approximation ratio of 0.651, surpassing the previous best of 0.614. The advantage persists even if the annealing procedure obtains a state whose energy is only 89% of its true ground state energy.
AI.conclusion: The approach opens a new route for hybrid quantum-classical algorithms that combine quantum with classical optimization methods, demonstrating robustness and improved approximation guarantees.

title: A hardware-safety-gated system for LLM-written native ARTIQ control code on a trapped-ion platform
summary: Large-language-model (LLM) agents can write and run experimental control code. This allows laboratory work to be conducted autonomously. However, this autonomy raises a safety problem that prior work has not addressed. Unchecked code can damage the apparatus, and there is no formal, per-operation boundary between human authorization/supervision, and agent decisions. We present a control system that places an LLM agent in the loop of a trapped-ion experiment while enforcing such a boundary. The agent controls the existing Advanced Real-Time Infrastructure for Quantum physics (ARTIQ) stack through tools provided by a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server. No tool call reaches the hardware unless it carries an authorization token bound to its exact contents. Tokens are issued in one of two ways: automatically, by running the agent's proposed script in an isolated hardware simulation (dax.sim) and checking every operation against preset per-device bounds, or manually by a human operator for sensitive actions. Within this boundary the agent develops its own experiments, rather than only calling pre-built routines. We deploy the system on a co-trapped $^{40}$Ca$^{+}$/$^{40}$CaOH$^{+}$ crystal, where the agent autonomously builds a full calibration stack and, with targeted operator guidance, closes a cross-instrument magnetic-field-stabilization loop. On a separate, independent $^{171}$Yb$^{+}$ platform, we confirm interface-level portability. We systematically test token-authorization mechanism with adversarial scripts that attempt to bypass it, mapping the precise boundary of its protection and prioritizing where to strengthen it next. Analyzing where the agent still requires human guidance, we find that its limits lie in metacognitive control, namely recognizing when a problem must be re-framed, rather than in domain knowledge.

AI.tldr: An LLM agent controls a trapped-ion experiment through a safety system that issues authorization tokens (via simulation checks or human approval) for each hardware operation, enabling autonomous experiment development while preventing damage.
AI.motivation: Prior LLM agent systems for lab automation lack safety boundaries—unchecked code can damage apparatus with no formal separation between human authorization and agent decisions.
AI.method: The system places an LLM agent in the loop of a trapped-ion experiment using an MCP server over the ARTIQ stack. Each tool call requires an authorization token bound to its contents, issued either automatically via hardware simulation (dax.sim) with per-device bound checks, or manually by a human operator for sensitive actions.
AI.result: The agent autonomously built a full calibration stack and closed a cross-instrument magnetic-field-stabilization loop on a co-trapped ⁴⁰Ca⁺/⁴⁰CaOH⁺ crystal. Interface-level portability was confirmed on a separate ¹⁷¹Yb⁺ platform. Adversarial token-authorization tests mapped protection boundaries.
AI.conclusion: The agent's limitations lie in metacognitive control (recognizing when a problem must be re-framed) rather than domain knowledge, indicating where future improvements are needed.

title: Quantum computer architecture with ions in tweezer arrays
summary: We propose a quantum computer architecture based on ions confined in optical tweezer arrays, combining the long coherence times of trapped-ion qubits with the reconfigurability and parallel operation enabled by tweezer platforms. Selected ions are transported to local interaction zones, where excitation to an auxiliary state with a displaced optical potential generates a controllable effective electric dipole. We develop and analyze entangling-gate mechanisms mediated by the Coulomb interaction between such effective dipoles, and show that they enable precise, temperature-robust closure of the center-of-mass and relative motional trajectories, leaving no residual entanglement between the qubits and the motion. We further outline a concrete implementation with barium ions based on state-selective polarizability, and study the suppression of cross-talk during parallel gate execution, with relevance to transversal gates in quantum error correction. Our results thereby establish a realistic route toward scalable ion-tweezer quantum processors.

AI.tldr: Proposes a scalable quantum computer architecture using ions in optical tweezer arrays, with entangling gates mediated by Coulomb interactions between effective electric dipoles, enabling temperature-robust, motion-free qubit operations for quantum error correction.
AI.motivation: To combine the long coherence times of trapped-ion qubits with the reconfigurability and parallel operation of optical tweezer platforms, aiming for a scalable quantum processor architecture.
AI.method: Ions are confined in optical tweezer arrays and transported to local interaction zones. Excitation to an auxiliary state with a displaced optical potential creates controllable effective electric dipoles. Entangling gates are mediated by the Coulomb interaction between these dipoles, enabling closure of motional trajectories without residual qubit-motion entanglement. A concrete implementation using barium ions with state-selective polarizability is outlined.
AI.result: The proposed gate mechanism achieves precise, temperature-robust closure of center-of-mass and relative motional trajectories with no residual qubit-motion entanglement. Cross-talk suppression during parallel gate execution is demonstrated, with relevance to transversal gates in quantum error correction.
AI.conclusion: The results establish a realistic and scalable route toward ion-tweezer quantum processors.

title: Particle-preserving fermionic shadows with mode-independent sample complexity
summary: We consider the problem of learning expectation values of particle-preserving operators with respect to an unknown $η$-particle $n$-mode fermionic state via classical shadows. Our main application is to estimating overlaps with arbitrary Slater determinant states: While it is known that such overlaps can, in the average case, be learnt to a fixed additive precision with a constant number of samples, the best-known worst case bound is $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt n \log n)$; here we improve this to $\mathcal{O}(η\logη)$, achieving a mode-independent sample cost. Our procedure is also computationally efficient, requiring only classical post-processing which for a generic dense orbital runs in time $\mathcal{O}(nη^2)$. For the task of estimating the expectation value of a general particle-preserving quadratic fermionic observable $h$, we prove a sample complexity bound of $\mathcal{O}(η\|h_0\|_2^2)$, where $h_0$ is the traceless component of $h$; the associated classical post-processing scales as $\mathcal{O}(n^2η)$. Finally, we discuss implementation of the required randomization: in a first-quantized encoding, approximate unitary designs give circuit depths polylogarithmic in the number of modes, contrasting with linear-depth requirements for nearest-neighbor second-quantized matchgate implementations. On the technical side, our proof reduces the extremal shadow variance to harmonic analysis on the AIII symmetric space $U(n)/(U(η)\times U(n-η))$ and evaluates the resulting integral using techniques from the theories of Jacobi ensembles and orthogonal polynomials, in a calculation which may be of independent interest.

AI.tldr: This paper improves worst-case sample complexity for learning overlaps with Slater determinants from $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt n \log n)$ to $\mathcal{O}(\eta \log \eta)$ using classical shadows, and proves sample complexity $\mathcal{O}(\eta \|h_0\|_2^2)$ for estimating expectation values of particle-preserving quadratic fermionic observables. The approach is computationally efficient and uses harmonic analysis on the AIII symmetric space.
AI.motivation: To learn expectation values of particle-preserving operators (especially overlaps with Slater determinants) for unknown fermionic states via classical shadows, improving worst-case bounds and achieving mode-independent sample cost.
AI.method: Classical shadows framework applied to fermionic states with particle-preserving operators; reduction of extremal shadow variance to harmonic analysis on the AIII symmetric space $U(n)/(U(\eta)\times U(n-\eta))$; integral evaluation using Jacobi ensembles and orthogonal polynomials.
AI.result: Sample complexity of $\mathcal{O}(\eta \log \eta)$ for learning Slater determinant overlaps (improving from $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt n \log n)$); $\mathcal{O}(\eta \|h_0\|_2^2)$ for general particle-preserving quadratic observables. Classical post-processing in $\mathcal{O}(n\eta^2)$ and $\mathcal{O}(n^2\eta)$ respectively.
AI.conclusion: Achieves mode-independent (worst-case) sample cost for Slater determinant overlaps and efficient classical post-processing; first-quantized encoding enables polylogarithmic-depth circuits via approximate unitary designs.

title: Large-scale multimode entangling-gate synthesis in trapped-ion systems
summary: Trapped-ion systems have emerged as a leading platform for scalable quantum information processing owing to their high-fidelity operations and long-range entangling capabilities. As the number of ions in a trap increases, the growing density of collective motional modes makes the synthesis of multimode entangling gates increasingly challenging. Designing large-scale gates requires simultaneously realizing the desired spin-spin interactions, suppressing residual spin-motion entanglement, and limiting experimental control resources, leading to a high-dimensional non-convex optimization problem. Here we develop a numerical framework for multi-tone gate synthesis that directly searches for control fields satisfying these competing requirements. By employing an alternating-minimization strategy, the framework improves numerical stability and remains effective for large systems with many motional modes and target interactions. As representative demonstrations, we synthesize gates implementing all-to-all and nearest-neighbor interaction patterns in ion chains of up to N = 1000, using only global laser control. Across the parameter regimes explored here, the control resources required to maintain high-fidelity interactions do not exhibit rapid growth with system size. We extend the framework to individual addressing using a structured qLDPC target at N = 512 as an example. These results identify multimode gate synthesis as a viable route toward programmable interaction engineering in large-scale trapped-ion quantum processors.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a numerical framework for multi-tone gate synthesis in trapped-ion systems, using alternating-minimization to design control fields that achieve desired spin-spin interactions while suppressing spin-motion entanglement. It demonstrates high-fidelity gates (all-to-all, nearest-neighbor, qLDPC) for chains up to N=1000 with only global laser control, showing control resources do not scale rapidly with system size.
AI.motivation: As trapped-ion systems scale up, the growing density of collective motional modes makes synthesizing multimode entangling gates increasingly challenging. Designing large-scale gates requires solving a high-dimensional non-convex optimization problem that simultaneously achieves desired spin-spin interactions, suppresses residual spin-motion entanglement, and limits experimental control resources.
AI.method: The authors develop a numerical framework using an alternating-minimization strategy to directly search for control fields satisfying the competing requirements of desired spin-spin interactions, residual spin-motion entanglement suppression, and limited control resources. The framework is applied to ion chains of up to N=1000 using global laser control, and extended to individual addressing using a structured qLDPC target at N=512.
AI.result: The framework successfully synthesizes gates implementing all-to-all and nearest-neighbor interaction patterns in ion chains up to N=1000 using only global laser control. Control resources required to maintain high-fidelity interactions do not exhibit rapid growth with system size across explored parameter regimes. The approach also works for individual addressing with a qLDPC target at N=512.
AI.conclusion: Multimode gate synthesis is a viable route toward programmable interaction engineering in large-scale trapped-ion quantum processors.

title: Quantum-Limited Subdiffraction Telescopy Requires Genuine Multi-Telescope Interference
summary: Conventional stellar interferometry reconstructs incoherent sources from pairwise mutual coherences between telescopes. Are such pairwise measurements sufficient for quantum-limited subdiffraction imaging with a telescope array? We show that for generic image-moment estimation, they are not. We consider weak incoherent light from a generic extended source observed by an array of telescopes, each supporting a single optical mode. For an N-telescope array, we derive the quantum Fisher information (QFI) scaling of image moments up to the cutoff 2N-2 and prove that arbitrary measurements restricted to telescope pairs attain the full-array QFI scaling only up to second order. Thus, estimating higher-order moments at the quantum limit requires genuinely multi-telescope interference. Inspired by spatial-mode demultiplexing (SPADE) from single-aperture subdiffraction imaging, we construct array-SPADE measurements that attain the optimal QFI scaling up to the finite-array cutoff. Finally, we show that these measurements can, in principle, be embedded in ancilla- and memory-assisted quantum-network architectures for long-baseline telescopy.

AI.tldr: For N-telescope arrays estimating image moments, pairwise (two-telescope) interference measurements are quantum-limited only up to second-order moments; estimating higher-order moments at the quantum limit requires genuine multi-telescope interference. The authors propose array-SPADE measurements achieving optimal QFI scaling up to the 2N-2 cutoff.
AI.motivation: To determine whether pairwise mutual coherence measurements (standard in stellar interferometry) are sufficient for quantum-limited subdiffraction imaging with a telescope array, or whether multi-telescope interference is fundamentally required.
AI.method: Derivation of quantum Fisher information (QFI) scaling for image moments up to order 2N-2; comparison of pairwise-measurement QFI to full-array QFI; construction of array-SPADE measurements inspired by single-aperture spatial-mode demultiplexing.
AI.result: Pairwise measurements achieve full-array QFI scaling only up to second order. For higher-order moments, multi-telescope interference is necessary. Array-SPADE measurements attain optimal QFI scaling up to the finite-array cutoff 2N-2.
AI.conclusion: Quantum-limited estimation of higher-order image moments demands genuine multi-telescope interference; such measurements can be embedded in ancilla- and memory-assisted quantum-network architectures for long-baseline telescopy.

title: Exploring dynamics of individual vortices in a superconductor via a levitated magnetic transducer
summary: Trapped vortices determine fundamental properties of superconductors and play an important role in many practical applications such as magnetic levitation, however their complex dynamics remain poorly understood. Here, we use the mechanical motion of micron-scale levitated magnetic particles to probe the dynamics of individual vortices. Specifically, we show that the dynamics of levitated magnets are strongly influenced by vortices trapped in the YBCO superconducting film. We observe random telegraph signals in the mechanical frequency, dissipation rate, and energy of levitated particles, which we attribute to random tunneling of individual vortices. The nonlinearity of vortex-defect interaction manifests as non-exponential decay in ringdown measurements, revealing a complex underlying potential landscape. Our results provide insights into elusive dissipation mechanisms in superconducting levitated systems, open new avenues for using levitated magnets as sensitive probes of static and dynamic properties of individual vortices in superconductors and their interactions with material disorder, and point toward novel routes for using magnetic particles as highly coherent mechanical transducers.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates that micron-scale levitated magnetic particles can probe individual vortex dynamics in YBCO superconducting films, revealing random telegraph signals and non-exponential relaxation that provide insights into vortex-defect interactions and dissipation mechanisms.
AI.motivation: Trapped vortices determine fundamental properties of superconductors and are important for applications like magnetic levitation, but their complex dynamics remain poorly understood.
AI.method: The authors use mechanical motion of micron-scale levitated magnetic particles to probe individual vortex dynamics in YBCO superconducting films, observing random telegraph signals in mechanical frequency, dissipation rate, and energy.
AI.result: Random telegraph signals attributed to random tunneling of individual vortices were observed; nonlinear vortex-defect interaction manifests as non-exponential decay in ringdown measurements, revealing a complex underlying potential landscape.
AI.conclusion: The results provide insights into dissipation mechanisms in superconducting levitated systems, open new avenues for using levitated magnets as sensitive probes of individual vortex properties, and point toward routes for using magnetic particles as highly coherent mechanical transducers.

title: Self-Sifting quantum key distribution
summary: In this paper, we introduce a novel two-way quantum key distribution (QKD) protocol in which the sender (Alice) and receiver (Bob) employ one qubit of a maximally entangled Bell state as the quantum channel for key exchange. The protocol incorporates a new security mechanism based on a scrambling operator. Unlike conventional two-way QKD protocols, all sifting operations and eavesdropper detection procedures are postponed until the completion of the quantum communication stage and are performed exclusively by Bob. Since the control mode is never publicly announced, attacks that rely on mode-dependent adaptations or attempt to remain hidden within the control mode are inherently prevented. Furthermore, the traveling qubit does not directly encode key information, substantially limiting the information that can be extracted from attacks targeting the quantum channel alone. An additional distinctive feature of the protocol is that rounds that would ordinarily be discarded can instead be utilized to detect the presence of an eavesdropper. We analyze a broad class of ancilla-based attacks, in which an eavesdropper couples an ancillary system to the transmitted qubit in an attempt to gain information about the key, and show that such attacks are detectable in their most general form.

AI.tldr: A novel two-way QKD protocol using a maximally entangled Bell state and scrambling operator that postpones all sifting and detection until after quantum communication, with Bob performing all control operations, preventing mode-dependent attacks and enabling discarded rounds for eavesdropper detection.
AI.motivation: To address security vulnerabilities in conventional two-way QKD protocols where public announcements of control mode enable mode-dependent attacks, and to improve protocol efficiency by reusing discarded rounds for eavesdropping detection.
AI.method: Employs one qubit of a maximally entangled Bell state as the quantum channel; incorporates a scrambling operator as a new security mechanism; defers all sifting and eavesdropper detection until after quantum communication, performed exclusively by Bob; traveling qubit does not directly encode key information.
AI.result: The protocol inherently prevents attacks that rely on mode-dependent adaptations; limits information extractable from attacks targeting the quantum channel alone; shows that a broad class of ancilla-based attacks are detectable in their most general form.
AI.conclusion: The proposed two-way QKD protocol offers enhanced security by eliminating mode-dependent attack surfaces and improving detection capabilities, with the scrambling operator and post-communication control mode serving as key security features.

title: Cultivating logical catalysts for fault-tolerant dyadic phase rotations
summary: We introduce a surface-code cultivation protocol for reusable logical catalyst states that implement exact fine dyadic phase gates $Z^{2^{-b}}$ by phase kickback. The catalyst is an eigenstate of a high-period Clifford circuit $U$, with a direct construction supported on $O(2^b)$ logical qubits. Once cultivated, each invocation implements the target phase through a controlled-$U$ gadget, removing Clifford+$T$ synthesis approximation error from the online gate and making the online non-Clifford depth independent of the target logical accuracy. As a concrete demonstration, we construct a catalyst for $\sqrt{T}=Z^{1/8}$, where $U$ is a nine-qubit brickwork Clifford circuit and controlled-$U$ consists of eight controlled-CNOTs. Starting from nine distance-three rotated-surface-code blocks, we cultivate the catalyst through logical-$U$ checks, syndrome extraction and postselection, code growth, and complementary-gap decoding. Due to the intrinsic fault tolerance of the phase read-out, a \emph{single} verification round already reaches the leading error-corrected scaling, in contrast to the repeated logical checks required when cultivating single-qubit magic states. A hybrid tensor-network and stabilizer simulation shows that, at physical error rate $p=10^{-3}$, the postselected catalyst can be grown to distance-seven rotated-surface-code blocks with logical leakage rate $\sim 10^{-6}$ using around seven expected attempts, and can be suppressed further with stronger postselection. Compared with existing protocols, our approach trades offline, phase-specific catalyst cultivation for exactness, reusability, and constant-depth online implementation of fixed fine dyadic phases in codes with restricted transversal gate sets.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a surface-code cultivation protocol for reusable logical catalyst states that implement exact fine dyadic phase gates $Z^{2^{-b}}$ via phase kickback. The catalyst is an eigenstate of a high-period Clifford circuit $U$, supported on $O(2^b)$ logical qubits. Each invocation uses a controlled-$U$ gadget, eliminating Clifford+$T$ synthesis approximation error and making online non-Clifford depth independent of target logical accuracy. A concrete $\sqrt{T}=Z^{1/8}$ catalyst uses a nine-qubit brickwork Clifford circuit with eight controlled-CNOTs. Starting from distance-three rotated-surface-code blocks, cultivation uses logical-$U$ checks, syndrome extraction, postselection, code growth, and complementary-gap decoding. A single verification round achieves leading error-corrected scaling. Hybrid tensor-network and stabilizer simulation at $p=10^{-3}$ shows postselected catalyst growth to distance-seven blocks with logical leakage rate $\sim 10^{-6}$ in ~7 attempts. The approach trades offline, phase-specific catalyst cultivation for exactness, reusability, and constant-depth online implementation of fixed fine dyadic phases in codes with restricted transversal gate sets.
AI.motivation: To eliminate Clifford+$T$ synthesis approximation error in non-Clifford gate implementation and reduce online non-Clifford depth, by cultivating reusable logical catalyst states that enable exact phase kickback for fine dyadic phase gates, overcoming limitations of single-qubit magic state distillation protocols that require repeated logical checks.
AI.method: The protocol constructs a catalyst as an eigenstate of a high-period Clifford circuit $U$ supported on $O(2^b)$ logical qubits. Each invocation applies a controlled-$U$ gadget for phase kickback. Cultivation starts from distance-three rotated-surface-code blocks and uses logical-$U$ checks, syndrome extraction, postselection, code growth, and complementary-gap decoding. A single verification round is sufficient due to intrinsic fault tolerance of phase read-out. Hybrid tensor-network and stabilizer simulation validates the approach.
AI.result: At physical error rate $p=10^{-3}$, the postselected catalyst can be grown to distance-seven rotated-surface-code blocks with logical leakage rate $\sim 10^{-6}$ using around seven expected attempts, and can be suppressed further with stronger postselection. The protocol removes Clifford+$T$ synthesis approximation error and achieves constant-depth online implementation.
AI.conclusion: The surface-code cultivation protocol offers exact, reusable, constant-depth online implementation of fine dyadic phase gates, trading offline, phase-specific catalyst cultivation for these advantages. It is particularly suited for codes with restricted transversal gate sets and outperforms existing magic state distillation approaches in terms of online overhead and exactness.
